questions.prompt: A lab task looks stuck. What does this workshop guarantee about every task and question?

options.text: Each task and question has a collapsed spoiler with the exact solution or expected output.
options.rationale: The teaching model is that a learner can never stay permanently stuck: spoilers are part of the lab contract.

options.text: Answers are withheld until a live quiz host reveals them at the end of the day.
options.rationale: Labs are standalone Markdown with spoilers; they do not depend on a live quiz service.

options.text: Tasks are unsolved on purpose so the room can sit a certification exam.
options.rationale: The workshop is aligned with CK* domains as a design check, not exam prep.

questions.explanation: Every lab task and question ships a <details> spoiler so a learner can unblock without waiting for a facilitator or a live quiz host.
questions.learningObjective: Use the spoiler contract instead of getting stuck on a lab step.

questions.prompt: Before applying any workload, Lab 00 asks you to confirm context and namespace. Why start there?

options.text: A valid kubeconfig can still point at the wrong cluster or namespace, so later applies land in the wrong place.
options.rationale: Pre-flight checks catch context and namespace mistakes before the first apply.

options.text: Every lab needs cluster-admin, so you must prove you can create nodes first.
options.rationale: Most labs are namespace-scoped; cluster-admin is not the default teaching model.

options.text: kubectl is optional if the live deck is open, so the check is only ceremonial.
options.rationale: Labs are applied with kubectl (or kind); the deck does not apply manifests for you.

questions.explanation: Lab 00 is a pre-flight: confirm the intended context and namespace so later labs do not mutate the wrong cluster.
questions.learningObjective: Verify kubeconfig context and namespace before the first apply.

questions.prompt: You change a COPY instruction in a Dockerfile. What happens to image layers?

options.text: That layer and every layer after it are rebuilt; earlier unchanged layers can still be cached.
options.rationale: Docker/OCI layer cache keys on the instruction and its inputs; a changed COPY busts that layer and all following ones.

options.text: The entire image is always rebuilt from scratch, including the base image download.
options.rationale: Unchanged earlier layers remain cache hits; the base image is not inherently re-pulled.

options.text: Only the COPY layer changes; later RUN layers keep their old cached result even if they used the copied files.
options.rationale: Later layers depend on the parent digest, so they cannot stay cached after the COPY layer changes.

questions.explanation: Image builds are a stack of layers. Changing COPY invalidates that layer and everything after it; earlier layers can still be reused.
questions.learningObjective: Explain how Dockerfile layer cache invalidation works.

questions.prompt: A Go service image is ~800 MB because the toolchain is in the same stage as the app. What is the applied fix this section teaches?

options.text: Build in one stage, then copy only the static binary into a tiny runtime stage.
options.rationale: Multi-stage builds keep compilers and module caches out of the image you run.

options.text: Schedule the fat image on a larger node so the extra packages do not matter.
options.rationale: Node size does not remove the toolchain from the attack surface or pull time.

options.text: Retag the same image as latest so Kubernetes pulls a smaller digest automatically.
options.rationale: Tags do not strip layers; latest is also a movable pointer, not a size fix.

questions.explanation: A build stage compiles the binary; the final stage copies only that artifact onto a minimal base so the toolchain never ships.
questions.learningObjective: Apply a multi-stage build so the runtime image does not contain the toolchain.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile runs curl with a token in the instruction itself. Why is that a supply-chain problem even after the build finishes?

options.text: The token is recorded in an image layer and in build history, so anyone with the image can recover it.
options.rationale: RUN/COPY layers persist. Secrets in instructions are not erased by later layers.

options.text: The token exists only in the builder's memory and cannot appear in the pushed image.
options.rationale: Build instructions and their outputs are part of the image unless you use a secret mount that never writes a layer.

options.text: Kubernetes will automatically convert that layer into a Secret object at pull time.
options.rationale: The platform does not scrape Dockerfile history into Secrets.

questions.explanation: Anything written into a layer stays in the image. Mount the secret at build time so it is used and never persisted.
questions.learningObjective: Keep build secrets out of image layers.

questions.prompt: A base image is referenced as alpine:3.20. What pinning practice does this section require for a reproducible, auditable runtime?

options.text: Pin the base by digest (sha256:…) so the exact bytes cannot move under the tag.
options.rationale: Tags are mutable. A digest names the image content.

options.text: Use alpine:latest so you always receive security patches without editing the file.
options.rationale: latest moves; it is the opposite of a pin and hides what you actually run.

options.text: Retag alpine:3.20 as alpine:prod on your laptop; the cluster will resolve that name to the same digest forever.
options.rationale: A local retag is not a content pin and is not what other machines will pull.

questions.explanation: Digest pins name the exact blob. Version tags can be moved by a rebuild of the same name.
questions.learningObjective: Pin container bases by digest rather than a movable tag.

questions.prompt: What does the Kubernetes control loop actually do?

options.text: Observe current state, diff it against desired state, act, and repeat.
options.rationale: Controllers reconcile: they do not run a one-shot script and exit.

options.text: SSH to each node once, start containers, and then forget them.
options.rationale: That is an imperative host model, not reconciliation.

options.text: Only the scheduler loops; kubelets and controllers apply objects once.
options.rationale: kubelets and controllers also continuously reconcile their objects.

questions.explanation: Desired state lives in the API. Controllers and kubelets repeatedly observe, diff, and act until reality matches.
questions.learningObjective: Describe reconciliation as observe, diff, act, repeat.

questions.prompt: You inspect a cluster. Where does desired state for a Deployment live, and where do the containers actually run?

options.text: Desired state is stored in the control plane (API server/etcd); containers run on worker nodes via kubelets.
options.rationale: The control plane holds objects; nodes run Pods.

options.text: Both desired state and containers live only on the node that first created the Pod.
options.rationale: Losing that node would lose the API objects; that is not how the control plane works.

options.text: Desired state lives in your local YAML files; the cluster never stores it.
options.rationale: kubectl apply writes objects into the API. Git may be a source, but the cluster stores the live object.

questions.explanation: etcd/API is the desired-state store. kubelets on nodes run the containers that realize that state.
questions.learningObjective: Separate control-plane desired state from node-level execution.

questions.prompt: You need a compact table of Pods, then the events and conditions for one Pod. Which pair of verbs matches that?

options.text: kubectl get for the list; kubectl describe for the object plus recent events.
options.rationale: get is the inventory; describe is the narrative including events.

options.text: kubectl apply twice — the second call prints events instead of applying.
options.rationale: apply writes objects; it is not an inspect tool.

options.text: kubectl exec is required because Pod status is only visible from inside the container.
options.rationale: Status and events are API data; exec is for a process in the container.

questions.explanation: get answers 'what exists'; describe answers 'what is going on with this object', including events.
questions.learningObjective: Choose get versus describe for inventory versus diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A JSONPath one-liner is the wrong tool for a first look at a misbehaving Pod. What should you do first?

options.text: Use get/describe (and optionally -o wide or -o yaml) to see status, IPs, and events before crafting a query.
options.rationale: Scavenger-hunt labs start with human-readable output, then narrow.

options.text: Delete the Pod immediately so the controller reprints a clean object.
options.rationale: Deleting destroys evidence; describe first.

options.text: kubectl edit the live object to add a debug sidecar before reading status.
options.rationale: You can inspect without mutating; edit is a later, deliberate change.

questions.explanation: Start with get/describe so you see phase, conditions, and events. JSONPath is for extracting a known field once you know what you are looking at.
questions.learningObjective: Inspect with get/describe before writing a custom query.

questions.prompt: A Pod's container exits and the kubelet restarts it. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The Pod identity stays the same while its container restart count increases.
options.rationale: A container restart within the Pod does not create a replacement Pod.

options.text: The kubelet creates a new Pod with a new UID.
options.rationale: A controller or user creates replacement Pods; a container restart alone does not.

options.text: Kubernetes creates a Deployment to preserve the workload.
options.rationale: Kubernetes does not infer a Deployment from a standalone Pod.

questions.explanation: The kubelet restarts containers according to the Pod restart policy; the Pod UID is unchanged.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a container restart from Pod replacement.

questions.prompt: Two containers in one Pod need to share a port namespace and talk on localhost. What is true?

options.text: Containers in a Pod share network namespace (and can share volumes); they are not separate Pods.
options.rationale: A Pod is one shared context: network, IPC, and optional volumes.

options.text: Each container gets its own Pod IP, so they must use a Service to reach each other.
options.rationale: The Pod has one IP; containers share it.

options.text: They can only share localhost if both are initContainers.
options.rationale: Init containers run first and exit; sharing localhost is a property of the Pod, not of init.

questions.explanation: A Pod is one network namespace. Sidecars and the main container share localhost; init containers run to completion first.
questions.learningObjective: Use the Pod as a shared network and volume context.

questions.prompt: You edit a Deployment's pod template. Which objects actually change underneath?

options.text: The Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet, which creates new Pods; the old ReplicaSet is scaled down.
options.rationale: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods is the ownership chain for a rollout.

options.text: Existing Pods are patched in place and keep the same names and UIDs.
options.rationale: Pod specs are mostly immutable; rollouts replace Pods.

options.text: Kubernetes creates a new Service so old and new Pods can run side by side forever.
options.rationale: A Service is independent; rollouts do not imply a new Service.

questions.explanation: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets. A template change starts a new ReplicaSet and rolls Pods from the old one to the new one.
questions.learningObjective: Explain Deployment, ReplicaSet, and Pod roles during a rollout.

questions.prompt: A rollout of a new image is unhealthy. What does this section teach as the immediate recovery?

options.text: Roll back to the previous Deployment revision so the last known ReplicaSet is scaled up again.
options.rationale: Deployments keep a revision history specifically so rollbacks are a first-class operation.

options.text: Delete the Deployment so kubelet recreates the old image from node cache.
options.rationale: Deleting the Deployment deletes its ReplicaSets and Pods; it is not a rollback.

options.text: Manually rename the old ReplicaSet; the Deployment will ignore the new one.
options.rationale: The Deployment owns ReplicaSet selection; renaming is not the supported rollback path.

questions.explanation: kubectl rollout undo (or an equivalent revert of the revision) scales the previous ReplicaSet back up.
questions.learningObjective: Recover from a bad rollout with a Deployment rollback.

questions.prompt: A Service has no ready endpoints although matching Pods are Running. What should you inspect first?

options.text: The Pods' readiness conditions and the Service selector.
options.rationale: EndpointSlices normally include ready matching Pods; readiness and selector mismatches are the direct checks.

options.text: Whether the Service uses NodePort.
options.rationale: Service type does not repair selector or readiness problems.

options.text: Whether the Pods share a ReplicaSet owner.
options.rationale: Service selection is label-based and independent of controller ownership.

questions.explanation: Services discover backends through selectors and EndpointSlices; unready or non-matching Pods do not become ready endpoints.
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the selector-to-EndpointSlice routing path.

questions.prompt: A frontend in the cluster must reach a backend without exposing the backend outside the cluster. Which Service type matches that intent?

options.text: ClusterIP — a virtual IP reachable from inside the cluster.
options.rationale: ClusterIP is the default in-cluster type; NodePort/LoadBalancer add off-cluster reachability.

options.text: NodePort — required whenever two Pods need to talk.
options.rationale: Pod-to-Service traffic uses ClusterIP; NodePort is for reaching from outside a node IP.

options.text: ExternalName — Kubernetes will copy the backend Pods onto a public hostname.
options.rationale: ExternalName is a DNS CNAME to an external name, not an in-cluster selector Service.

questions.explanation: Pick Service type by who needs to reach the workload. In-cluster only means ClusterIP.
questions.learningObjective: Choose a Service type from the intended clients.

questions.prompt: You apply an Ingress object and nothing answers on the hostname. What is the usual missing piece?

options.text: An Ingress controller must be running to implement the rules; the API object alone does not proxy traffic.
options.rationale: Ingress is a spec. A controller (Contour, ingress-nginx, …) programs a proxy.

options.text: CoreDNS automatically becomes an HTTP reverse proxy when it sees an Ingress.
options.rationale: CoreDNS answers cluster DNS; it does not implement Ingress.

options.text: A Service mesh is required before any Ingress object can be created.
options.rationale: Ingress does not depend on a mesh.

questions.explanation: Applied ≠ working. Watch the controller (and its LoadBalancer/address) before blaming the YAML rules.
questions.learningObjective: Treat Ingress as rules that a controller must implement.

questions.prompt: Two hostnames must hit different Services through one controller. Which Ingress fields carry that routing intent?

options.text: rules[].host and http.paths (including pathType) bound to a backend Service.
options.rationale: Host + path + pathType are the portable Ingress routing surface.

options.text: A hardcoded Pod IP in the Ingress, because Services cannot be Ingress backends.
options.rationale: Ingress backends are Services, not Pod IPs.

options.text: spec.gatewayClassName on the Ingress object.
options.rationale: gatewayClassName is Gateway API, not Ingress.

questions.explanation: An Ingress lists host and path rules. pathType (Prefix, Exact, ImplementationSpecific) is part of the rule, not an annotation afterthought.
questions.learningObjective: Route two hostnames with Ingress host, path, and pathType.

questions.prompt: Who chooses which GatewayClass a Gateway uses?

options.text: The Gateway author sets spec.gatewayClassName.
options.rationale: GatewayClass selection is explicit in the Gateway specification.

options.text: Whichever controller starts first becomes the default.
options.rationale: Gateway API does not select a class by controller startup order.

options.text: Each HTTPRoute chooses the GatewayClass directly.
options.rationale: Routes attach to Gateways; the Gateway selects the GatewayClass.

questions.explanation: A Gateway references one GatewayClass by spec.gatewayClassName; Routes attach to the resulting Gateway listeners.
questions.learningObjective: Explain the GatewayClass, Gateway, and HTTPRoute ownership boundary.

questions.prompt: An HTTPRoute is applied but traffic never arrives. The Gateway shows Programmed=False with AddressNotAssigned on kind. What should you conclude?

options.text: Read Gateway/HTTPRoute status (Accepted, Programmed, ResolvedRefs): kind often has no cloud load balancer, while the proxy may still be reachable via port-forward.
options.rationale: The section teaches status conditions as the diagnosis, including AddressNotAssigned on kind.

options.text: Gateway API cannot run on kind; convert the HTTPRoute back to an Ingress automatically.
options.rationale: The lab runs Gateway API on kind with a conformant controller.

options.text: Set gatewayClassName on the HTTPRoute to force an address.
options.rationale: HTTPRoute does not select GatewayClass; it attaches to a Gateway.

questions.explanation: Gateway API surfaces why a route is not serving: Accepted, Programmed, ResolvedRefs. AddressNotAssigned on kind is expected without a cloud LB.
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose Gateway API using status conditions rather than guessing.

questions.prompt: You change a ConfigMap that is injected as environment variables. When do running containers see the new values?

options.text: Not until the Pod is recreated (for example a rollout); env is fixed at container start.
options.rationale: Environment variables are not live-reloaded from a ConfigMap update.

options.text: Immediately in every process, because the API server rewrites /proc/environ.
options.rationale: The kernel environment of a running process is not rewritten by a ConfigMap patch.

options.text: ConfigMaps never affect env; only Secrets can be environment variables.
options.rationale: Both ConfigMaps and Secrets can populate env.

questions.explanation: envFrom/valueFrom is snapshotted at start. File mounts can update in place; many apps still need a rollout (often a checksum annotation) to reload.
questions.learningObjective: Contrast ConfigMap env injection with mounted-file updates.

questions.prompt: A database password must be injected into the same app that already uses a ConfigMap for non-sensitive settings. What belongs in a Secret?

options.text: The credential — stored as a Secret and referenced separately from the ConfigMap.
options.rationale: Secrets are the API for sensitive values; ConfigMaps are for non-secret config.

options.text: The password in the ConfigMap, because encryption at rest is identical for both objects.
options.rationale: Even when etcd encryption is enabled, the teaching split is still Secret vs ConfigMap; do not put passwords in ConfigMaps.

options.text: The password baked into the image so Kubernetes never stores it.
options.rationale: That puts the secret in every layer and every registry copy — the S02 anti-pattern.

questions.explanation: Keep non-secret config in a ConfigMap and credentials in a Secret. Same injection styles (env or volume), different object.
questions.learningObjective: Split non-secret config from credentials across ConfigMap and Secret.

questions.prompt: Which object is the workload's request for storage, and which object is the actual volume?

options.text: PersistentVolumeClaim is the request; PersistentVolume is the volume that binds to it.
options.rationale: PVC is namespaced demand; PV is the cluster volume; StorageClass describes how to provision.

options.text: The Pod names a PersistentVolume directly; claims are optional metadata.
options.rationale: Workloads mount claims, not raw PVs, in the usual dynamic-provisioning path.

options.text: A StorageClass is the mounted volume; PVC and PV are only billing records.
options.rationale: StorageClass is a provisioner template, not a mounted volume.

questions.explanation: PVC → PV (often via StorageClass) is the binding chain. The Pod mounts the claim.
questions.learningObjective: Name the PVC, PV, and StorageClass roles.

questions.prompt: A Deployment used emptyDir for app data. After a Pod replace, the files are gone. What change makes the data survive that replace?

options.text: Replace emptyDir with a PVC mount so a new Pod can reattach the same claim.
options.rationale: emptyDir dies with the Pod. A bound PVC outlives the Pod.

options.text: Scale to three replicas so emptyDir is copied between them automatically.
options.rationale: emptyDir is per-Pod and is not replicated by scaling.

options.text: Mount the node root with hostPath so data lives on the node filesystem forever.
options.rationale: hostPath ties data to one node and is a security foot-gun, not the PVC lesson.

questions.explanation: Swap emptyDir for a claim. The PVC stays; replacement Pods mount it again (subject to access mode and scheduling).
questions.learningObjective: Persist data across Pod replacement with a PVC.

questions.prompt: What does a StatefulSet give each replica that a Deployment does not?

options.text: A stable ordinal name, stable DNS, and (with volumeClaimTemplates) its own PVC.
options.rationale: web-0, web-1, … plus per-ordinal storage and DNS are the StatefulSet contract.

options.text: Nothing — StatefulSet is only a rename of Deployment for marketing.
options.rationale: Identity and storage semantics differ.

options.text: One shared PVC that every replica must write at the same path concurrently by default.
options.rationale: volumeClaimTemplates mint one PVC per ordinal, not one shared disk, unless you design that separately.

questions.explanation: StatefulSet identity is ordinal: hostname, DNS, and usually a dedicated claim per replica.
questions.learningObjective: State the stable-identity contract of a StatefulSet.

questions.prompt: Peers must resolve each replica as web-0.web, web-1.web, not a single ClusterIP. What Service is required?

options.text: A headless Service (clusterIP: None) that the StatefulSet references by serviceName.
options.rationale: Headless Services publish per-Pod DNS instead of one virtual IP.

options.text: A LoadBalancer Service, because ordinal DNS only exists behind a cloud IP.
options.rationale: Per-Pod DNS is a headless Service feature, independent of LoadBalancer.

options.text: No Service: StatefulSet creates DNS names from the Pod UID alone.
options.rationale: The governing Service name is part of the StatefulSet spec and DNS scheme.

questions.explanation: clusterIP: None plus serviceName gives stable per-Pod DNS for the set.
questions.learningObjective: Attach a headless Service so StatefulSet replicas have per-Pod DNS.

questions.prompt: What do CPU/memory requests do versus limits?

options.text: Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits are the runtime ceiling the kubelet/cgroup enforces.
options.rationale: That is the requests-schedule / limits-enforce split taught in the section.

options.text: They are aliases; Kubernetes uses whichever number is larger.
options.rationale: They are distinct fields with distinct effects.

options.text: Limits are used only at schedule time; requests are ignored after the Pod binds.
options.rationale: The scheduler keys off requests; limits apply at runtime.

questions.explanation: Without requests the scheduler cannot reserve capacity. Limits cap usage (CPU throttle or memory OOM).
questions.learningObjective: Separate scheduling requests from runtime limits.

questions.prompt: A container exceeds its memory limit. What happens, compared with exceeding a CPU limit?

options.text: Memory over limit is typically OOM-killed; CPU over limit is throttled, not killed for that reason.
options.rationale: cgroup memory max vs cpu quota behave differently.

options.text: Both CPU and memory over-limit always SIGKILL the container immediately.
options.rationale: CPU quota throttles; it does not by itself OOM-kill.

options.text: Limits are advisory; the kubelet never kills or throttles.
options.rationale: Limits are enforced.

questions.explanation: Right-sizing starts from that difference: CPU throttle vs memory eviction/OOM.
questions.learningObjective: Predict throttle versus OOM from CPU vs memory limits.

questions.prompt: What question does a readiness probe answer versus a liveness probe?

options.text: Readiness: should this Pod receive traffic? Liveness: is the process wedged and should it be restarted?
options.rationale: They are different questions; collapsing them is a classic misconfiguration.

options.text: They are the same probe with two names for historical reasons.
options.rationale: They have different kubelet actions.

options.text: Readiness restarts the container; liveness only removes Endpoints.
options.rationale: That swaps the two actions.

questions.explanation: Failed readiness → not a ready endpoint. Failed liveness → kubelet restarts the container. Startup delays both until boot succeeds.
questions.learningObjective: Separate readiness (traffic) from liveness (restart).

questions.prompt: A slow-booting app is killed in a restart loop even though it would become healthy after 90 seconds. Which probe is the applied fix?

options.text: A startup probe that delays liveness and readiness until boot succeeds.
options.rationale: startupProbe exists so liveness does not fire during a long start.

options.text: A more aggressive liveness probe so the kubelet 'gives up faster'.
options.rationale: That makes the restart loop worse.

options.text: Remove readiness so unready Pods still receive traffic during boot.
options.rationale: That sends traffic to a process that is not ready.

questions.explanation: startupProbe covers slow boot. Until it succeeds, liveness and readiness are held back.
questions.learningObjective: Use a startup probe to protect slow boots from liveness restarts.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a Job and a CronJob?

options.text: A Job runs to completion once; a CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule.
options.rationale: CronJob is a factory for Jobs.

options.text: A CronJob is a Deployment that restarts every minute.
options.rationale: CronJobs create Jobs, not long-running ReplicaSets.

options.text: A Job keeps a replica Running forever; a CronJob is only for one-shot debug Pods.
options.rationale: Jobs are finite; Deployments are the long-running controller.

questions.explanation: Job = run until Complete/Failed. CronJob = schedule that creates those Jobs, with history and concurrency controls.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a one-shot Job from a scheduled CronJob.

questions.prompt: A nightly Job sometimes still runs when the next schedule fires. Which CronJob field prevents overlapping runs?

options.text: concurrencyPolicy: Forbid (skip the new run while the previous Job is still active).
options.rationale: Forbid, Allow, and Replace are the three concurrency policies.

options.text: spec.completions on the CronJob itself, which pauses the schedule.
options.rationale: completions belongs on the Job template, not as a CronJob schedule lock.

options.text: An HPA on the CronJob so extra schedules become extra replicas of the same Job.
options.rationale: HPA does not manage CronJob concurrency.

questions.explanation: concurrencyPolicy: Forbid skips a tick when a prior Job is still running. Replace would delete the old one; Allow would overlap.
questions.learningObjective: Keep a CronJob schedule safe with concurrencyPolicy.

questions.prompt: An HPA is targeting CPU utilization at 50%. What must the workload have for that metric to be meaningful?

options.text: A CPU request on the target Pods, because utilization is relative to the request.
options.rationale: HPA CPU % is current usage / request, not / limit and not an absolute core count.

options.text: A GPU limit, because HPA can only scale on extended resources.
options.rationale: The default resource metric is CPU/memory, not GPU.

options.text: Nothing — HPA reads replica count from etcd and ignores metrics-server.
options.rationale: HPA needs metrics (typically metrics-server) and resource requests for resource metrics.

questions.explanation: Without a CPU request, resource utilization cannot be computed as a percentage of requested CPU.
questions.learningObjective: Tie HPA CPU targets to Pod resource requests.

questions.prompt: Load spikes for 20 seconds, replicas jump, then immediately scale back, then jump again. What HPA behavior is the section pointing at?

options.text: Stabilization windows (and related scale-up/scale-down policies) exist to stop that flapping.
options.rationale: HPA behavior has scale-up/down stabilization so a brief spike does not thrash replica count.

options.text: Delete the HPA whenever load is bursty; only Deployments can handle bursts.
options.rationale: The fix is policy, not removing autoscaling.

options.text: Set CPU request to 0 so utilization is always 100% and the replica count stays pegged at max.
options.rationale: A zero request is invalid/meaningless for this metric and does not stabilize.

questions.explanation: HPA is another reconcile loop. Stabilization keeps replica count from chasing noise.
questions.learningObjective: Use HPA stabilization to avoid replica flapping.

questions.prompt: Pod Security Standards describe profiles such as restricted. What is restricted actually evaluating?

options.text: Fields on the Pod (securityContext, capabilities, volume types, …) against a documented profile.
options.rationale: PSS is a policy over Pod spec fields, enforced by admission (PSA) or other policy engines.

options.text: Whether the node OS vendor is on an allow-list.
options.rationale: PSS is not a node-vendor check.

options.text: Whether the image has zero CVEs in a scanner database.
options.rationale: Image scanning is a different control than PSS.

questions.explanation: restricted rejects root, privilege escalation, extra capabilities, missing seccomp, and similar Pod fields.
questions.learningObjective: Describe Pod Security Standards as a Pod-spec profile.

questions.prompt: You set runAsNonRoot: true but the image's default user is still UID 0. What happens under restricted?

options.text: Admission may pass the field check, then the container fails at runtime because UID 0 violates the promise — pin runAsUser to a non-root UID in the image.
options.rationale: runAsNonRoot is a promise the image (or runAsUser) must keep.

options.text: The kubelet silently remaps UID 0 to 65534 without any spec change.
options.rationale: There is no automatic UID remap as the default teaching path.

options.text: restricted allows UID 0 when runAsNonRoot is true, because the flag is documentation only.
options.rationale: The combination is inconsistent and fails.

questions.explanation: restricted wants a non-root user. The image must actually run as one; set runAsUser (and the image USER) accordingly.
questions.learningObjective: Make runAsNonRoot true in both the spec and the image.

questions.prompt: A NetworkPolicy selects backend Pods and allows ingress from app=frontend on TCP 8080. What happens to other ingress?

options.text: Once an ingress policy selects those Pods, unspecified ingress is denied (on a policy-capable CNI).
options.rationale: NetworkPolicy is allow-list once it applies; default-open becomes default-deny for that direction.

options.text: Everything else remains allowed; NetworkPolicy can only add extra allows, never deny.
options.rationale: Selecting a pod with an ingress policy isolates it.

options.text: kube-proxy implements NetworkPolicy by deleting Services.
options.rationale: NetworkPolicy is CNI/dataplane, not Service deletion.

questions.explanation: Pick Pods, then allow listed sources/ports. Other ingress to those Pods is refused if the CNI enforces NetworkPolicy.
questions.learningObjective: Treat NetworkPolicy as isolation plus explicit allows.

questions.prompt: You apply a correct NetworkPolicy on a cluster whose CNI does not implement NetworkPolicy. What do you observe?

options.text: The object exists but traffic is not fenced — policy needs a policy-capable CNI.
options.rationale: The section warns that NetworkPolicy is not enforced by every CNI.

options.text: The API server always rejects NetworkPolicy unless Calico is built into kube-apiserver.
options.rationale: The API accepts the object regardless of CNI.

options.text: CoreDNS stops resolving until you delete the policy.
options.rationale: A backend ingress policy does not by itself disable DNS.

questions.explanation: Kind labs that teach NetworkPolicy use a CNI that enforces it. On a non-policy CNI the YAML is a no-op.
questions.learningObjective: Require a policy-capable CNI before trusting NetworkPolicy.

questions.prompt: RBAC grants a permission when which three pieces are joined by a binding?

options.text: A subject (who), verbs, and resources — bound to a Role or ClusterRole.
options.rationale: Role/ClusterRole lists verbs×resources; RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding attaches subjects.

options.text: A Secret token alone; bindings are optional metadata.
options.rationale: A token authenticates; authorization still needs RBAC rules.

options.text: A node label selector; RBAC is scheduling, not authorization.
options.rationale: Node selectors are not RBAC.

questions.explanation: who × verb × resource, tied by a binding. Namespace Roles stay in one namespace; ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped (or used via RoleBinding).
questions.learningObjective: Describe RBAC as subject, verb, resource, and binding.

questions.prompt: You created a Role and a ServiceAccount. Workloads still get Forbidden. What object is missing?

options.text: A RoleBinding (or ClusterRoleBinding) that subjects the ServiceAccount to that Role.
options.rationale: Without a binding, the Role is unused.

options.text: A Kubernetes User object in etcd named after the ServiceAccount.
options.rationale: ServiceAccounts are already API subjects; there is no separate User CR for them.

options.text: You must convert the Role into a ClusterRole or the API ignores it.
options.rationale: Namespaced Roles are valid; they just need a RoleBinding in that namespace.

questions.explanation: Role + ServiceAccount + RoleBinding is the three-object pattern the lab applies. auth can-i / impersonation verifies it.
questions.learningObjective: Bind a Role to a ServiceAccount before expecting authorization to succeed.

questions.prompt: What three files make a minimal Helm chart as taught here?

options.text: Chart.yaml, values.yaml, and at least one template (for example templates/deployment.yaml).
options.rationale: Chart metadata, default values, and templates are the chart.

options.text: Only a Dockerfile; Helm infers a chart from the image name.
options.rationale: Helm packages Kubernetes YAML, not Dockerfiles.

options.text: Only a CRD named HelmRelease; templates are optional.
options.rationale: HelmRelease is a Flux (or similar) CR; a chart itself is the three-file layout.

questions.explanation: Chart.yaml names the chart, values.yaml supplies defaults, templates render Kubernetes objects.
questions.learningObjective: Identify the files that constitute a Helm chart.

questions.prompt: You want to see what a chart would apply without contacting the cluster, then validate against the API without installing. Which pair matches?

options.text: helm template (local render) then helm install/upgrade --dry-run=server (or equivalent client/server dry-run) to validate.
options.rationale: template never needs a cluster; server dry-run talks to the API without persisting a release.

options.text: helm uninstall --keep-history is the only safe preview.
options.rationale: Uninstall is not a preview.

options.text: helm has no render path; you must kubectl run the chart tarball.
options.rationale: helm template is the local render path taught in the section.

questions.explanation: Render locally, then dry-run against the API. install/upgrade then create numbered revisions you can roll back.
questions.learningObjective: Preview a chart with helm template and API dry-run before install.

questions.prompt: In the GitOps model this section teaches, where is desired state, and how does the cluster change?

options.text: Git holds desired state; an in-cluster agent pulls and reconciles the cluster toward that Git spec.
options.rationale: GitOps is pull-based reconciliation with Git as the source of truth, independent of Argo CD vs Flux.

options.text: Engineers must kubectl apply from laptops; Git is only a wiki.
options.rationale: That is push-based imperative apply, the thing GitOps replaces as the control loop.

options.text: CI must SSH to nodes and docker run the new tag.
options.rationale: That bypasses both Git and the Kubernetes API.

questions.explanation: Git is spec. The agent (Argo CD Application or Flux Kustomization/HelmRelease) pulls and reconciles. GitOps is a discipline, not a product.
questions.learningObjective: State GitOps as Git-as-desired-state with a pull agent.

questions.prompt: Someone kubectl-ed a replica count in the cluster that disagrees with Git. Self-heal is on. What happens?

options.text: The agent reverts the live object toward Git; the Git spec wins.
options.rationale: Self-heal is reconciliation with Git as spec.

options.text: The agent commits the live replica count back to Git automatically.
options.rationale: Default self-heal does not treat the cluster as the source of truth.

options.text: Kubernetes keeps both values forever because Git and the API are unrelated stores.
options.rationale: The agent continuously diffs and acts.

questions.explanation: Sync/Ready is not the same as application health, but self-heal specifically restores Git's desired spec.
questions.learningObjective: Predict self-heal when live state drifts from Git.

questions.prompt: What two pieces make an operator, as this section defines it?

options.text: A CRD that extends the API, plus a custom controller that reconciles those objects.
options.rationale: Operator = new kind (CRD) + loop (controller).

options.text: A Helm chart with no new API types.
options.rationale: A chart installs existing kinds; that is not the operator pattern.

options.text: A kubectl plugin that prints YAML, with no in-cluster loop.
options.rationale: A plugin is not a controller.

questions.explanation: The CRD registers the kind. The controller observes custom resources and acts. Maturity goes from install to autopilot.
questions.learningObjective: Define an operator as CRD plus custom controller.

questions.prompt: You apply a Custom Resource whose Spec asks for a child Deployment. Who is supposed to create that Deployment?

options.text: The operator's controller, in its reconcile loop, from the CR spec.
options.rationale: You declare intent on the CR; the controller creates children.

options.text: kube-scheduler, because Spec is a scheduling hint.
options.rationale: The scheduler places Pods; it does not implement your CRD.

options.text: etcd, via a built-in trigger on any CRD name ending in Operator.
options.rationale: etcd stores objects; it does not reconcile your domain.

questions.explanation: A custom resource is declared intent. The controller observe→diff→act until children match spec.
questions.learningObjective: Treat a custom resource as spec for a controller, not as a scheduler hint.

questions.prompt: What does a ServiceMonitor declare to the Prometheus Operator?

options.text: Intent to scrape a Service's named metrics port (for example /metrics on port web).
options.rationale: ServiceMonitor is scrape intent; the operator generates Prometheus scrape config.

options.text: Only Alertmanager routes; it never scrapes.
options.rationale: Alertmanager has its own CR; ServiceMonitor is scrape selection.

options.text: It replaces node-exporter with a sidecar in every Pod.
options.rationale: node-exporter is a cluster metrics source, not what ServiceMonitor is.

questions.explanation: You name the Service port and path. The operator writes scrape config; Prometheus then has a target.
questions.learningObjective: Use ServiceMonitor as scrape intent for the Prometheus Operator.

questions.prompt: Prometheus has no target for your app even though /metrics works on the Pod. The ServiceMonitor looks right. What is a likely miss from this section?

options.text: The Service port is not named (or the name does not match the ServiceMonitor), so the operator cannot select the scrape port.
options.rationale: The walkthrough names the metrics port and points ServiceMonitor at that name.

options.text: You must delete the Prometheus CRD so Prometheus falls back to file_sd.
options.rationale: Deleting the CRD removes the operator's API, it does not fix discovery.

options.text: ServiceMonitor only works if the app is exposed via Ingress.
options.rationale: Scrape is in-cluster to the Service; Ingress is unrelated.

questions.explanation: Give the metrics port a name on the Service, then reference that name from the ServiceMonitor. The operator generates scrape config from that pair.
questions.learningObjective: Name the Service metrics port so a ServiceMonitor can select it.

questions.prompt: Which combination is taught as 'own the node' from inside a Pod?

options.text: privileged plus hostPath: / (the host filesystem mounted in).
options.rationale: Those two levers are the escape hatch the section shows, then removes.

options.text: A failing readiness probe, because NotReady Pods gain node API access.
options.rationale: Readiness does not grant host access.

options.text: A ConfigMap mounted at /etc, because ConfigMaps are always hostPath.
options.rationale: ConfigMaps are not host mounts.

questions.explanation: privileged + host root mount is node takeover. Drop both, then apply restricted fields, so admission can reject the escape Pod.
questions.learningObjective: Name privileged and hostPath:/ as the node-escape pair.

questions.prompt: A namespace enforces restricted Pod Security Admission. You apply the escape Pod (privileged + hostPath /). What should happen?

options.text: Admission rejects it before the Pod exists; the escape never runs.
options.rationale: PSA restricted is the gate that holds the line in the lab.

options.text: The Pod runs, then kubelet notices and deletes it after one probe.
options.rationale: Restricted PSA is admission-time, not a post-start killer.

options.text: restricted only logs; privileged Pods always schedule.
options.rationale: enforce: restricted denies.

questions.explanation: The hardened Pod is what restricted admits. The escape Pod is rejected at admission.
questions.learningObjective: Rely on PSA restricted to reject a privileged hostPath Pod.

questions.prompt: The capstone 'will it stay up?' pass adds which runtime trio to a bare container?

options.text: Resource requests/limits, probes, and graceful shutdown (preStop / terminationGracePeriodSeconds).
options.rationale: Those three are the stay-up walkthrough: QoS, traffic/restarts, drain in-flight work.

options.text: Only an HPA; probes and resources are optional once replicas exist.
options.rationale: HPA without requests/probes is not the capstone lesson.

options.text: hostNetwork: true so kube-proxy cannot drop the Pod.
options.rationale: hostNetwork is not a reliability default.

questions.explanation: Stay up: reserve and cap resources, gate traffic and restarts with probes, drain before SIGKILL.
questions.learningObjective: List resources, probes, and graceful shutdown as the stay-up baseline.

questions.prompt: The capstone still shows image: app:latest and no securityContext. What is the applied fix for those two gaps?

options.text: Pin the image by digest (or an immutable tag you control) and set a restricted-compatible securityContext.
options.rationale: Mutable tags and missing securityContext are the 'can you run it / is it safe' misses.

options.text: Keep latest so production always self-patches; skip securityContext on Deployments.
options.rationale: latest is not a pin; Deployments still need a securityContext for restricted.

options.text: Add only a PDB; image tags and securityContext are out of scope for best practices.
options.rationale: PDBs matter, but they do not replace pinning or securityContext.

questions.explanation: Best practices stack the earlier sections: pin what you run, and give the Pod a securityContext that can pass restricted.
questions.learningObjective: Replace mutable tags and missing securityContext in a production-shaped workload.

questions.prompt: How does this workshop treat CKAD/CKA domains?

options.text: As a design checklist for coverage — not as an exam dump or the organizing principle of the days.
options.rationale: AGENT.md and the wrap-up: alignment, not exam prep.

options.text: As a question bank copied from live exams so participants can memorize answers.
options.rationale: That is explicitly out of scope and against the quiz rules.

options.text: The domains are ignored; only vendor product labs matter.
options.rationale: The wrap-up maps domains as a checklist, vendor-neutrally.

questions.explanation: CK* domains help check that the superset covers the field. Delivery is still the red line plus labs, not a cram course.
questions.learningObjective: Use CK* domains as a coverage checklist, not as exam prep.

questions.prompt: A participant asks to schedule Operator dev 101 (kubebuilder) as part of the canonical three-day cut. What is the honest status?

options.text: S24 is deferred and not schedulable until a Go/kubebuilder toolchain session can validate it; it is not in the canonical authored cut.
options.rationale: Manifest status is deferred; docs must not claim it is taught in the three-day delivery.

options.text: S24 is a core Day-3 lab and is already fully authored.
options.rationale: That contradicts the deferred status.

options.text: S24 is authored but hidden only because quizzes are missing.
options.rationale: It is deferred for toolchain reasons, not quizzes.

questions.explanation: Wrap-up points at skipped/advanced material. S24 remains deferred; do not advertise it as a schedulable lab.
questions.learningObjective: State that S24 is deferred and not part of the schedulable cut.
